source: Hand-curated catalog of workforce policy archetypes. Expanded from the Windfall Trust Policy Atlas (Labor Market Adaptation, 2024) and research-anchored dimension-shift signatures.

policies.name: Sector-Based Training (Healthcare)
policies.tagline: Project QUEST–style sectoral training pipeline targeting healthcare occupations
policies.description: Multi-year cohort training programs that prepare workers for specific healthcare roles (nursing assistants, medical technicians, allied health) with wraparound services, employer partnerships, and guaranteed placement.
policies.evidence: Project QUEST (San Antonio) RCT: +30% earnings 9 years post-program. Targets adaptability — measured to nearly eliminate the displaced-worker scarring effect in healthcare.
workforceImpacts: Pays displaced and entry-level workers a stipend during 12–24 months of healthcare credentialing
Places graduates with employer partners (hospital systems, clinics) at agreed entry wages
Reduces healthcare workforce shortages while creating mobility ladders for low-wage workers
Tracks 9-year wage gains of +30% vs. control (Project QUEST RCT)

policies.name: AI Literacy / GenAI Fluency (Statewide)
policies.tagline: Universal community-college + library-based AI tool training, 6-week certificate
policies.description: Statewide rollout of a 6-week certificate course on practical generative AI usage in office settings — prompting, verification, workflow integration. Offered through community college network and public libraries.
policies.evidence: Brynjolfsson, Li, Raymond 2025 (5,172 customer-support agents): 15% productivity gain from AI tools, 30% for least-experienced. Effect concentrated in workers who actually use the tools — training closes the usage gap.
workforceImpacts: Equips incumbent office workers across all sectors with a portable AI-fluency credential
Closes the within-firm usage gap (currently ~50% of workers with access don't use AI tools)
Boosts measured per-worker productivity 15–30%, with biggest gains for less-experienced workers
Universal access via community colleges + libraries; reaches workers who'd never enroll in formal training

policies.name: Registered Apprenticeship (Manufacturing)
policies.tagline: Earn-and-learn programs partnered with regional employers in advanced manufacturing
policies.description: Federal/state registered apprenticeships placing workers with manufacturers; 18–36 months of paid on-the-job training plus classroom hours. Targets reskilling for AI-augmented manufacturing roles.
policies.evidence: USDOL apprenticeship outcome studies: 91% retention, +$300K lifetime earnings vs. non-apprentices. Boosts adaptability for workers transitioning into AI-augmented production roles.
workforceImpacts: Earn-and-learn structure: workers earn full wages while completing 2–4 years of OJT + classroom
Builds reskilling pipeline for AI-augmented manufacturing roles (CNC operators, robotics technicians)
91% retention rate; ~$300K lifetime earnings advantage vs. non-apprentices (USDOL)
Anchors workers in region — apprentices typically stay with sponsoring employer

policies.name: Wage Insurance (Statewide)
policies.tagline: Displaced workers receive 50% of wage loss for up to 24 months when re-employed at lower pay
policies.description: Modeled on Trade Adjustment Assistance wage insurance. Reduces the personal cost of taking a lower-wage adjacent role, softening the transition for displaced workers and increasing re-employment speed.
policies.evidence: Hyman 2018 (TAA wage insurance): increased re-employment probability by 10pp for displaced workers; modest wage gains; sharp reduction in long-term unemployment.
workforceImpacts: Replaces 50% of wage loss for up to 24 months when displaced workers re-employ at lower pay
Cuts long-term unemployment sharply (+10pp re-employment probability within 6 months)
Lets workers accept adjacent lower-wage roles without devastating household income
Particularly effective for older displaced workers facing >20% wage cuts post-displacement
targetPopulations: Workers 50+ facing re-employment at lower wages

policies.name: Occupational Licensing Reform
policies.tagline: Streamline state-level licensing barriers in healthcare, finance, and construction
policies.description: Targeted reform of state occupational licensing — reciprocal recognition across states, scope-of-practice expansion (e.g., nurse practitioners), and removal of redundant credentials. Lowers the regulatory drag on adoption AND on worker mobility.
policies.evidence: Kleiner-Krueger studies on licensing: state licensing reduces interstate worker mobility by ~7% and slows technology diffusion in regulated sectors. Reform yields measurable adoption acceleration.
workforceImpacts: Removes redundant credential barriers in healthcare, finance, and construction trades
Cross-state reciprocal recognition lets workers relocate without re-credentialing (~7% mobility lift)
Expands scope-of-practice for nurse practitioners, dental hygienists, paralegals — meeting demand without lengthy retraining
Frees workers from being trapped in occupational silos as their narrow specialty automates
targetPopulations: Workers in adjacent occupations who could fill demand with lighter credentialing

policies.name: Public AI Compute Access (SMB)
policies.tagline: State-run AI compute infrastructure for small/medium businesses
policies.description: State-sponsored shared AI infrastructure (subsidized API access, training, security review) for SMBs that can't afford in-house deployment. Lowers cost and trust barriers; speeds adoption in long-tail sectors.
policies.evidence: BTOS data shows AI adoption concentrated in large firms (250+ employees adopt at 3× the rate of <50). McElheran et al. 2024: shared infrastructure could close half this gap.
workforceImpacts: Lets SMBs adopt AI without absorbing security review and infrastructure costs that only large firms can afford
Closes the firm-size adoption gap (250+ employee firms currently adopt at ~3× the rate of <50)
Workers at small firms gain access to the same AI productivity tools as workers at Fortune 500s
Indirectly preserves SMB jobs by keeping small firms competitive against AI-enabled larger competitors
targetPopulations: Workers at small and mid-size firms

policies.name: Employer Retraining Tax Credit
policies.tagline: Refundable credit for firms that retrain incumbent workers displaced by AI
policies.description: Refundable federal/state tax credit covering 50% of training costs up to $5K/worker for firms that retrain incumbent workers for AI-augmented roles within current employment. Modeled on Georgia's longstanding Retraining Tax Credit.
policies.evidence: Georgia Retraining Tax Credit (since 1998) shows real uptake at modest scale; effectiveness depends on credit size and employer awareness. Limited rigorous evidence for AI-specific applications.
workforceImpacts: Cuts firms' financial barrier to retraining incumbent workers in-place rather than displacing them
Keeps workers with current employer through technology transition (reduces involuntary churn)
Particularly impactful for SMBs that can't absorb training costs out of pocket
Modest absolute effect — credit must be large enough to actually change employer behavior
targetPopulations: Incumbent workers facing AI-driven role change

policies.name: Public Sector Job Guarantee (Pilot)
policies.tagline: Government as employer-of-last-resort offering public-service jobs to anyone unable to find work
policies.description: Regional pilot job guarantee: government offers a public-service job (community care, infrastructure, environmental services) at a living wage to any worker unable to find private employment within 6 months of displacement. Modeled on Argentina's Jefes y Jefas (2002) and various municipal guarantees in the US.
policies.evidence: Jefes y Jefas (Argentina, 2002): reduced extreme poverty by 25% in participating households. Federal job guarantee at national scale is fiscally heavy ($400B+/yr CBO range); pilot scale is more tractable. Limited US RCT evidence.
workforceImpacts: Hard floor under displaced workers' incomes — eliminates the long-term unemployment trap
Builds public goods (eldercare, climate adaptation, urban repair) that markets underprovide
Removes the leverage employers gain from the threat of unemployment in wage bargaining
Politically and fiscally heavy lift — typically pilot scale and time-limited
targetPopulations: Displaced workers in regions with weak private labor demand

policies.name: Four-Day Workweek (Productivity Sharing)
policies.tagline: Reduce standard workweek to 32 hours; convert AI productivity gains into leisure rather than displacement
policies.description: Mandate or incentivize a 32-hour standard workweek for full-time employees, on the premise that AI productivity gains should partly accrue to workers as time rather than as layoffs or wage stagnation. Iceland and UK pilots show maintained output with significantly higher wellbeing.
policies.evidence: Iceland 2015–2019 trial (2,500 workers): productivity maintained or improved, wellbeing significantly higher. UK 2022 trial (61 firms): 92% continued the policy after the pilot. Effects vary widely by sector.
workforceImpacts: Distributes AI productivity gains as leisure across workers, reducing displacement pressure on any single role
Lower hours per worker means more workers needed for the same total output
Wellbeing and retention gains documented in multiple sectoral pilots
Hardest to implement in shift-based and 24/7 customer-facing sectors; easier in knowledge work

policies.name: Worker Voice in AI Adoption (Sectoral Bargaining)
policies.tagline: Codified collective bargaining over AI deployment in target sectors
policies.description: Codify worker rights to bargain over AI deployment decisions: advance notice of automation, retraining commitments, severance for displaced workers, and worker consent for performance monitoring. Modeled on European works councils and the SAG-AFTRA / WGA 2023 Hollywood AI agreements.
policies.evidence: SAG-AFTRA 2023 contract established AI consent and compensation requirements. German co-determination correlates with slower but more stable adoption. Effects on net employment ambiguous; effects on wage preservation and worker voice are strong.
workforceImpacts: Slows adoption to a pace workers can absorb; reduces shock-displacement events
Advance notice and retraining commitments soften individual transition costs
Workers gain compensation for AI-derived productivity, not just employers
May modestly slow productivity growth — trade-off for better distribution
targetPopulations: Unionized workers in healthcare, education, entertainment

policies.name: Regional Skill Gap & Exposure Infrastructure
policies.tagline: Continuous regional AI exposure measurement that targets workforce dollars to highest-need pockets
policies.description: Build state/regional capacity for ongoing AI exposure measurement at the occupation × employer level. Outputs feed local workforce board funding decisions, employer transparency, and worker advisory services. Lightweight policy that increases the precision of all OTHER policies.
policies.evidence: Cost-effective enabling infrastructure. Hard to attribute jobs to directly, but multiplies the effectiveness of training and adjustment programs. Comparable to existing MSA labor market intelligence units (e.g., regional WIBs in CA, MA).
workforceImpacts: Surfaces displacement risks at occupation level before they become layoffs
Lets workforce boards target dollars where they'll actually move the needle
Gives workers data to make career decisions in advance
Multiplier on other policies — sharper data makes every intervention more effective

policies.name: Lifelong Learning Account (LiLA)
policies.tagline: Portable, government-matched accounts for ongoing skills training over a working lifespan
policies.description: Individual accounts where worker, employer, and government each contribute ~$750/yr (= $2.25K/yr total) toward training, credentialing, or career-change expenses. Worker-controlled and portable across employers. Modeled on Singapore SkillsFuture and the UK Lifelong Learning Entitlement.
policies.evidence: Singapore SkillsFuture (since 2015) reaches ~50% of working-age citizens annually. UK 2023 LLE pilot ongoing. US Individual Training Accounts under WIOA show smaller-scale uptake but positive effects on completion when paired with case management.
workforceImpacts: Continuous funding flow for skills development — not just at displacement moments
Worker-controlled and portable across jobs — fits gig, contract, and short-tenure employment
Reaches workers who never engage with formal workforce programs
Outcomes depend on training quality — accounts alone don't guarantee good labor market returns

policies.name: Displaced-Worker Entrepreneurship Support
policies.tagline: Microgrants, coaching, and benefits-bridge for displaced workers starting businesses
policies.description: Bundled support for displaced workers transitioning to self-employment: $5-25K microgrants, 12-month UI benefits bridge via Self-Employment Assistance, business coaching, and community capital access. Federal SEA program exists but only 8 states participate.
policies.evidence: Self-Employment Assistance program (since 1993): 2-3x business survival rates vs. control in participating states. SBA SCORE mentoring + microloan combos show similar effects. Scale is limited by program awareness and complexity.
workforceImpacts: Lets displaced workers create their own jobs rather than wait for re-employment
Bridges income gap during business startup phase via UI continuation
Capital + coaching combination addresses both money and know-how gaps
Self-employment isn't right for everyone — selection on motivation and capability matters
